![Image 1: John Badman|The Telegraph Edwardsville continues to heal and learn from the Dec. 10, 2021 tornado that killed six people when it struck an Amazon fulfillment center. City council members paused their meeting this week for a moment of silence in memory of those killed in the storm. Edwardsville Police and Fire Departments say the storm has provided lessons for them. ](https://www.theintelligencer.com/news/article/In-Its-Wake-lessons-learned-a-year-after-17638626.php)

![Image 2: John Badman|The Telegraph The Amazon warehouse in Edwardsville where six people died a year ago has been repaired and is one of the multiple Amazon warehouse facilities in the area.](https://www.theintelligencer.com/news/article/In-Its-Wake-lessons-learned-a-year-after-17638626.php)

Left: Edwardsville continues to heal and learn from the Dec. 10, 2021 tornado that killed six people when it struck an Amazon fulfillment center. City council members paused their meeting this week for a moment of silence in memory of those killed in the storm. Edwardsville Police and Fire Departments say the storm has provided lessons for them. Right: The Amazon warehouse in Edwardsville where six people died a year ago has been repaired and is one of the multiple Amazon warehouse facilities in the area. Photos: John Badman | The Telegraph

Edwardsville continues to heal and learn from the Dec. 10, 2021 tornado that killed six people when it struck an Amazon fulfillment center. Photos: John Badman | The Telegraph

What lessons have been learned 12 months after an EF-3 tornado plowed through an Amazon Fulfillment Center in Edwardsville?

Edwardsville Police and Fire personnel responded quickly to the incident, which occurred during the evening of Dec. 10, 2021. Per the National Weather Service (NWS), multiple severe thunderstorms formed ahead of an approaching cold front during the late afternoon and evening. Other storm features included tornadoes, large hail and damaging winds.

NWS forecasters said the tornado formed south of Interstate 270 and three-fourths of a mile west of the 270-255 interchange. The funnel moved northeast and rapidly intensified, first hitting the west-facing walls of the structure.

According to reports, six Amazon employees took shelter in the wrong designated bathroom for safety when the warehouse walls and roof collapsed, killing them.

The victims included Austin McEwen, 26, of Edwardsville; Clayton Cope, 29, of Alton; Larry Virden, 46 of Collinsville; DeAndre Morrow, 28, of St. Louis; Kevin Dickey, 62, of Carlyle; and Etheria Hebb, 24, of St. Louis.

Article continues below this ad

![Image 3: Austin McEwen](https://www.theintelligencer.com/news/article/In-Its-Wake-lessons-learned-a-year-after-17638626.php)

Austin McEwen

McEwen family

“The immediate aftermath of the tornado was hectic for quite some time,” recalled Edwardsville Police Chief Michael Fillback. “Once we made it past that point, we were able to sit down with the fire department to discuss the overall response. Those discussions will help make the response to a similar incident run efficiently.”

“In the fire service, we review incidents of all sizes,” said city Fire Chief James Whiteford. “There are always lessons to be learned from these types of events. Reliable communication is a necessity in any emergency, so we have since purchased new responder radios that will ensure our ability to communicate now and well into the future.”

The weather that Friday was unusually warm for mid-December. The highs reached the upper 70s with a strong southerly to southwesterly wind; such conditions were usually found in late April or early May, not 15 days before Christmas. Earlier in the week, local meteorologists predicted severe weather for Dec. 10, including the possibility of tornadoes. By mid-day, the area was in the Moderate category for tornadoes, the second-highest level on a scale of five.

A tornado rated a three on the [Enhanced Fujita Scale](https://www.theintelligencer.com/projects/guide/enhanced-fujita-ef-tornado-scale/), (EF-3) has rotational winds of between 136 and 165 miles per hour. Per the NWS, the tornado was on the ground for five minutes with an estimated peak wind speed of 150 miles per hour and the twister traveled for about 4.3 miles. Per the NWS, the western walls of the site collapsed inward, triggering other structural failures as the twister rotated through the warehouse. It collapsed other walls and tore through a large segment of the roof.

In April, Aaron Priddy, an area director with the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) in Fairview Heights, said based on employee interviews, some Amazon workers did not know where the designated shelter-in-place area was during emergencies. In September, the Intelligencer reported that the warehouse site will be rebuilt “to pre-loss conditions” according to a permit filed with Edwardsville. Amazon does not own the fulfillment center; an anonymous individual owns the site.

“Some employees were unaware the designated tornado shelter was the restroom located in the northern portion of the building and instead took shelter in the restroom located in the southern portion of the building,” an OSHA letter dated April 26, 2022, read.

“It was unfortunate to learn that the Edwardsville Amazon facility was again built without Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) shelters when FEMA shelters can prevent a tragedy like this, where six people needlessly died, especially in an area prone to tornadoes,” said Alice McEwen, the mother of McEwen, an Amazon delivery driver who died in the storm.

McEwen graduated from Collinsville High School and moved to Edwardsville after graduation.

In the storm’s wake, there was an outcry from some people that Amazon put its holiday and end-of-year profits ahead of its employees’ safety and media outlets released copies of text messages between delivery drivers and dispatchers and texts between Virden and his girlfriend, Cherie Jones.

“Amazon has the resources to equip their facilities with FEMA shelters,” said the McEwens’ attorney, Jack Casciato. “The McEwens had hoped Amazon would have improved the site safety at this specific Amazon facility. Adding these types of shelters is one of several means that could improve site safety in Tornado Alley.”

Casciato claims McEwen was told to go back to the Amazon facility despite winds increasing in the area that December afternoon. He claims McEwen was directed to take shelter in a bathroom with five others when the concrete structure collapsed on them.

Contegra Construction, which built the original warehouse in 2017, issued a statement about five months after the tornado. An excerpt from it reads, “The applicable building code adopted by the municipality where the warehouse is located requires the project’s design professional to design the building to withstand 90-mile-per-hour ‘straight-line’ winds. The tornadic winds generated by the EF-3 tornado that directly hit the Amazon warehouse were determined to have reached a wind speed of at least 150 miles per hour.”

On July 5, 2022, the Edwardsville City Council unanimously approved a motion to adopt the 2021 International Building Code (IBC), replacing the 2006 IBC previously used, as part of a lengthy slate of code updates from committee meetings in late June.

State Rep. Katie Stuart, D-Edwardsville, on Friday released a statement noting the anniversary of the tragedy.

Article continues below this ad

"One year ago, our community was struck by a devastating tornado that took the lives of six Amazon workers and left an indelible mark on our community," the statement read. "For the family and friends of those who were lost, the pain from this tragedy may never fully fade, but neither will the memory of those individuals who lost their lives.

"I believe that every worker deserves a safe and healthy work environment and I am committed to being a champion for workers’ safety and well-being," she said. "It is important that corporations such as Amazon implement and enforce safety measures, as well as provide their workers with ongoing training and support, and listen to and address the concerns of our workers.

Article continues below this ad

"I will always stand with our community and do everything possible both to honor the lives of those who were lost and prevent such losses from occurring in the future.”

Corporate public relations representatives with Amazon did not respond to questions by this story's deadline.

![Image 4: Families of those who died in the fatal Dec. 10, 2021 collapse of the Amazon warehouse facility in Edwardsville continue to deal with their losses. Pictured are Carla and Lynn Cope, center, of Brighton, the parents of Clayton Lynn Cope, 29, of Alton, who was killed in the building collapse.](https://www.theintelligencer.com/news/article/In-Its-Wake-lessons-learned-a-year-after-17638626.php)

![Image 5: Ambulances and fire trucks line up along the west side of the Amazon warehouse on South Gateway Commerce Center Drive in Edwardsville on Dec. 10, 2021, after a tornado swept through the area, collapsing the walls of the building. ](https://www.theintelligencer.com/news/article/In-Its-Wake-lessons-learned-a-year-after-17638626.php)

![Image 6: This Dec. 11, 2021, satellite photo provided by Maxar shows a close-up of an Amazon warehouse in Edwardsville, Ill., after severe storms moved through the area late the previous evening, causing catastrophic damage. (Satellite image ©2021 Maxar Technologies via AP)](https://www.theintelligencer.com/news/article/In-Its-Wake-lessons-learned-a-year-after-17638626.php)

Left: Families of those who died in the fatal Dec. 10, 2021 collapse of the Amazon warehouse facility in Edwardsville continue to deal with their losses. Pictured are Carla and Lynn Cope, center, of Brighton, the parents of Clayton Lynn Cope, 29, of Alton, who was killed in the building collapse. Top right: Ambulances and fire trucks line up along the west side of the Amazon warehouse on South Gateway Commerce Center Drive in Edwardsville on Dec. 10, 2021, after a tornado swept through the area, collapsing the walls of the building. Bottom right: This Dec. 11, 2021, satellite photo provided by Maxar shows a close-up of an Amazon warehouse in Edwardsville, Ill., after severe storms moved through the area late the previous evening, causing catastrophic damage. (Left and Top right photos by John Badman. Bottom right photo: Satellite image ©2021 Maxar Technologies via AP.)

Top: Families of those who died in the fatal Dec. 10, 2021 collapse of the Amazon warehouse facility in Edwardsville continue to deal with their losses. Pictured are Carla and Lynn Cope, center, of Brighton, the parents of Clayton Lynn Cope, 29, of Alton. Middle: Ambulances and fire trucks line up along the west side of the Amazon warehouse on South Gateway Commerce Center Drive in Edwardsville on Dec. 10, 2021, after a tornado swept through the area. Bottom: This Dec. 11, 2021, satellite photo provided by Maxar shows a close-up of an Amazon warehouse in Edwardsville, Ill., after severe storms moved through the area late the previous evening, causing catastrophic damage. (Left and Top right photos by John Badman. Bottom right photo: Satellite image ©2021 Maxar Technologies via AP.)

Fillback, a 27-year veteran of the police department, described how the various natural disaster trainings have assisted his department.

“The training that we do has helped us better understand what types of obstacles or dangers we might face responding to these types of incidents,” he said. “National Incident Management trainings help us identify how to put together a chain of command to speed up the process of getting resources where they need to be and identifying what additional resources we need to request. These types of incidents are impossible for one person to manage, and the training helps us prepare to coordinate our efforts to allow for quicker and more efficient decision-making.”

Whiteford agreed.

“Training is the best way to prepare for emergencies; planning for and training on disaster situations is a key component of the emergency preparedness concept,” he said. “In Edwardsville, we try to have one large-scale training each year for city administrative personnel. These trainings help to improve coordination among departments like police, fire and public works. They aid in understanding the priorities and needs of other departments in the city that are necessary to keep essential services functioning for the community.”

After it moved away from the Amazon site, the tornado continued moving northeast, across Sand Road, where it shredded an unanchored mobile home, an outbuilding and snapped trees and downed power poles. The storm moved over South University Drive and crossed into the Sunset Hills Country Club before lifting back up into the clouds just west of Butler Boulevard five minutes after initially touching down. Storm investigators noted that debris from the warehouse was found along the entire track of the storm, which ended tens of miles away.

Per the NWS, “Since 2000, there have been only 13 F/EF2+ tornadoes across the entire states of Missouri and Illinois in December. The only other December tornado outbreak on record in our county warning area to have more than 3 tornadoes rated F/EF2 or greater was on Dec. 18, 1957.”

“As a police department we always try to learn from the incidents we face,” Fillback said. “We try to take into account things such as, better perimeter setup and staging points. Additionally, these types of situations garner a lot of media attention. In this incident, our dispatch center was inundated with phone calls and emails, while still trying to handle radio traffic, 911 and other calls for service. That was a challenge, but it offered valuable insight into how we need to handle that in the future.”

Article continues below this ad

“I am proud of the way our city responded to this event. Fire, EMS, police and public works employees worked together seamlessly in the field, and we had great support from city administration, especially the finance and IT departments,” Whiteford said. “The public and local businesses were helpful as well. One of the lessons we learned was that management of donations can be challenging in situations like this. The community pulled together and generously offered all sorts of assistance. It’s important to be able to effectively coordinate, track and quickly direct that where it needs to go.”

Dec 10, 2022

![Image 7: Photo of Charles Bolinger](https://www.theintelligencer.com/news/article/In-Its-Wake-lessons-learned-a-year-after-17638626.php)

Charles Bolinger wrote for The Edwardsville Intelligencer from 2018 through 2024. He covered Edwardsville, Glen Carbon, Maryville, Edwardsville Township and the Collinsville School District. He is a graduate of Webster University in St. Louis.

SPRINGFIELD, Ill. (AP) — The family of a delivery driver who died last month when a [tornado collapsed](https://apnews.com/article/tornado-amazon-facility-collapse-llinois-4ba2dbe420ac27c6828f4ee4edb036f6) the central Illinois Amazon facility where he worked filed a wrongful death lawsuit Monday in Madison County.

The action on behalf of Austin McEwen, 26, claims that Amazon failed to warn employees of dangerous weather or provide safe shelter before a tornado slammed the Edwardsville facility Dec. 10, killing McEwen and five others.

It is believed to be the first legal action taken in response to the deaths. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration has [opened an investigation](https://apnews.com/article/tornadoes-technology-business-workplace-safety-illinois-a5238e8413ae999ce30a183d5ac3c62d).

McEwen’s parents, Randy and Alice McEwen, allege that Amazon administrators knew severe weather was imminent but had no emergency plan nor evacuated employees from the fulfillment center.

“Sadly, it appears that Amazon placed profits first during this holiday season instead of the safety of our son and the other five,” Alice McEwen said at a news conference Monday.

Amazon “carelessly required individuals ... to continue working up until the moments before the tornado struck,” the lawsuit says, and “improperly directed” McEwen and colleagues to shelter in a rest room, which it says the company knew or should have known wasn’t safe.

“They had people working up to the point of no return,” said Jack Casciato, the McEwens’ lawyer who is a partner of Clifford Law Offices.

Amazon spokeswoman Kelly Nantel released a statement that countered that the lawsuit “misunderstands key facts” including the differences among severe weather alerts and the condition and safety of the building.

[](https://apnews.com/article/tornadoes-business-lawsuits-weather-illinois-6f9b008c595ddb7681dde136b7fec74e)

“This was a new building less than four years old, built in compliance with all applicable building codes, and the local teams were following the weather conditions closely,” Nantel said. “Severe weather watches are common in this part of the country and, while precautions are taken, are not cause for most businesses to close down. We believe our team did the right thing as soon as a warning was issued.”

The lawsuit seeks more than $50,000 from each of the four defendants named in the suit, which includes Amazon.com, the construction company that built the facility and the project’s developer.

Nantel said the company would defend itself against the lawsuit but would continue to focus on “supporting our employees and partners, the families who lost loved ones, the surrounding community, and all those affected by the tornadoes.”
